title: Strictification and Mac Lanes Coherence Theorem

items.title: Canonical morphisms between parenthesised tensor words
Why 'every diagram commutes' is false as stated
The category of binary words
The category of binary words is monoidal
items.strategy: Use the empty word as unit and the binary-word concatenation operation as tensor. Since there is exactly one morphism between words of equal length and none otherwise, functoriality and the pentagon and triangle reduce to uniqueness of the relevant length-preserving arrows.

items.title: The category of right-module endofunctors
The right-module endofunctor category is strict monoidal
items.strategy: Tensor two objects by composing their underlying endofunctors and using the source's evident composite for the right-module structure map. Composition of endofunctors is literally associative and unital, so the associator and unitors are identities.

items.title: Mac Lane strictification
items.strategy: Send an object X to left multiplication X tensor -, with the associator supplying the right-module structure. Show every right-module endofunctor is isomorphic to one of this form via evaluation at the unit, prove fullness and faithfulness from the component at the unit, and then read off the strong monoidal structure maps from the unitors and associator.

items.title: Strictification gives equivalence, not on-the-nose identification
A monoidal category equivalent to a strict one satisfies coherence
items.strategy: Transport any canonical-map diagram along the given monoidal equivalence into the strict target, where every canonical map built from associators and unitors is an identity. Faithfulness of the underlying equivalence then reflects equality of the transported composites back to the original category.

items.title: Strictification itself costs no Choice, but skeletal strictification does
Mac Lane coherence in canonical-map form
items.strategy: Apply the generic converse theorem to the specific strictification equivalence of this page. In the strict target every canonical map between the same source and target is an identity, so the original canonical maps are forced to agree.

items.title: The coherence theorem's exact scope
Unbracketed tensor strings are well defined after coherence
items.strategy: Define an unbracketed n-fold tensor expression by choosing any parenthesisation and use the coherence theorem to show that all choices are canonically and uniquely identified. Later pages may then suppress the brackets, but only through this theorem.

items.title: The monoid-object axioms may be written without associators
items.strategy: Translate the explicitly bracketed monoid-object diagrams through the strictification equivalence, where the associator and unitors are identities, and then transport the simplified equalities back. The coherence theorem shows the resulting unbracketed formulas are independent of the parenthesisation choices that were suppressed.

items.title: The word category is the free monoidal category on one generator
items.strategy: Interpret the generating word in a target monoidal category by a chosen object and extend recursively over the binary-word tensor. The coherence theorem supplies the unique image of each length-preserving arrow, so the recursive assignment extends to a unique strong monoidal functor.

items.title: The free-word formulation implies the canonical-map formulation
items.strategy: Evaluate the unique arrow in the free monoidal category between two binary words of the same length at the ordered list of objects under discussion. The induced natural transformation is exactly the canonical map, so uniqueness in the free category yields uniqueness of canonical maps in every monoidal category.

items.title: The historical route to coherence and the route authored here
Every diagram in a monoidal category commutes
items.strategy: Contrast the source's formal-diagram theorem with the stronger blanket slogan. Once two different formal vertices evaluate to the same object, arbitrary noncanonical endomorphisms can be inserted and need not commute.

items.title: Every monoidal category is isomorphic to a strict one
items.strategy: The strictification theorem gives only a monoidal equivalence, and the page's nontrivial associator example shows that no isomorphism of monoidal categories need exist. The refutation is therefore exactly the gap between equivalence and isomorphism.

items.title: Every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a skeletal strict one
items.strategy: The page's boundary remark separates ordinary strictification from the extra representative-choosing step needed to make a category skeletal. The same example that blocks isomorphism also blocks the stronger claim that these two simplifications can always be achieved at once.

items.title: Coherence says that any two parallel morphisms in a monoidal category are equal
items.strategy: Unwind the theorem's quantifiers: it only compares canonical morphisms built from associators and unitors between parenthesisations of one ordered list. Arbitrary parallel morphisms are outside that scope.

items.title: Strictification requires the axiom of choice
items.strategy: Separate the explicit Cayley/Yoneda strictification construction from the later skeletal refinement. The first is built functorially from the given monoidal category, while the second requires selecting representatives.

title: Strictification and Mac Lanes Coherence Theorem — Examples

items.title: The two routes around the pentagon are equal
items.strategy: Write the two composites between the extreme four-fold bracketings and observe that both are canonical morphisms with the same source and target. The coherence theorem then identifies them.

items.title: A canonical map between two bracketings of a five-fold product
items.strategy: Choose two explicit five-fold parenthesisations and write one chain of associators joining them. The coherence theorem shows that any other chain gives the same natural isomorphism.

items.title: The word category on words of length three
items.strategy: List the two binary words of length three and the unique arrow between them in each direction. This makes the free-word category concrete before the general freeness theorem is used elsewhere.

items.title: Strictification of a cartesian monoidal category computed
items.strategy: Take the cartesian monoidal structure from finite products and compute the strictification functor X maps to X times -. The module-structure maps are the evident reassociations of products, so the abstract construction becomes explicit.

items.title: Two formally distinct words can become the same object
items.strategy: Use a strict monoidal category with an object carrying a nonidentity endomorphism. Distinct formal words then evaluate to the same object, and a square using a noncanonical endomorphism shows why the blanket slogan 'every diagram commutes' fails.

items.title: A monoid object written with and without associators
items.strategy: Start from the explicit associator-bearing diagrams in the monoid-object definition, then rewrite them using the coherence theorem's unbracketed notation. The example makes the gain from strictification visible without changing the underlying mathematics.
